[[File:Helliwells - Lady Look Ahead - 1939 - 2.jpg|thumb|Advertisement in ''[[Flight International|Flight]]'' magazine, June 1939]]
'''Helliwells Ltd''' was a British engineering company.  The company was founded in [[Dudley]], Worcestershire, in 1889 as a manufacturer of fireplace accessories.  It branched out into the automotive and aerospace sectors as these experienced growth in the early 20th century.  In 1939 it established a factory at [[Walsall Aerodrome]], which it used during the [[Second World War]] to adapt the American-made [[Douglas A-20 Havoc|A-20 Havoc/Boston]] to British standards and to refurbish [[Spitfire]], [[Supermarine Seafire|Seafire]] and [[North American T-6 Texan|Harvard]] aircraft.

In the post-war years, Helliwells purchased [[Swallow Sidecar Company|Swallow Coachbuilding]] and from 1946 to 1951 produced the [[Swallow Gadabout]] motor scooter and prototypes of the [[Triumph TR-X]] motor car.  Helliwells was purchased by [[TI Group|Tube Investments Group]] in 1950, and from 1954 to 1955 produced the [[Swallow Doretti]] luxury motor car.  Helliwells was renamed TI Hollow Extrusions in 1985 and, after its sale to the former managing director of [[Reynolds Technology|Reynolds Tube]], was known as  Hay Hall Tyseley.  The company was dissolved in 2011.

== History ==
===Origins ===
[[File:Helliwells 1920 advertisement.jpg|thumb|A 1920 advertisement featuring fireplace accessories]]
Helliwells was established in 1889 at Fountain Street, [[Dudley]], in the [[Black Country]] and was originally a manufacturer of [[fire iron]]s and fireguards; the company was first registered on 26 June 1899.<ref name=smith/><ref name=companies/>  With the growth of the motor car industry the company branched out into folded metalwork for windscreen frames.  By the late 1930s, with the expansion of the [[Royal Air Force]], it had entered the aerospace industry as a manufacturer of windscreens and cabin tops.<ref name=cooper>{{cite news |last1=Cooper |first1=David |title=The sports car built at a Black Country airport |url=https://www.pressreader.com/uk/black-country-bugle/20240522/281582360743701?srsltid=AfmBOop7Cx8iyAqzLoJO90OiKxvcuDtk2bqqUlcvyUn8GmKJ8QcXSUnX |access-date=12 October 2024 |work=Black Country Bugle |date=22 May 2024}}</ref>  To further its ambitions in this sector it negotiated permission from the [[Walsall Corporation]] to lease land at [[Walsall Aerodrome]] for construction of  a factory.<ref name=cooper/><ref>{{cite book |title=The Metal Industry |date=July 1937 |publisher=Louis Cassier Company |page=631 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=Y6XmAAAAMAAJ |language=en}}</ref>  This was completed by 1939, by which time Helliwells had offices, a store and a tool shop at Fountain Street, Dudley, a 3-storey factory at Oakeywell Street, Dudley, additional offices in Walsall and the new works at Walsall Airport where it hoped to consolidate all its operations.<ref>{{cite book |title=Flight and the Aircraft Engineer: Official Organ of the Royal Aero Club |date=1939 |page=176 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=AYDpwMstwWoC |language=en}}</ref>

=== Second World War ===
[[File:Top Hangar - Aldridge Airport - geograph.org.uk - 5500497.jpg|thumb|Top Hangar at Walsall Aerodrome, with sign reading "Helliwells Ltd Plane Parts 1938-56"]]
During the Second World War Helliwells was designated as a British "sister" firm of the American [[Douglas Aircraft Company]].  Helliwells worked to adapt Douglas' [[Douglas A-20 Havoc|A-20 Havoc/Boston]] aircraft to British standards and to install additional equipment for service with the Royal Air Force.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Brew |first1=Alec |title=Boulton Paul Aircraft Since 1915 |date=29 May 2020 |publisher=Fonthill Media |page=139 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=1vfnDwAAQBAJ |language=en}}</ref>  In this role Helliwells initially worked under the direction of a technical committee at British manufacturer [[Boulton Paul Aircraft]], but from 4 June 1943 worked under its own technical committee.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Postan |first1=Michael Moïssey |last2=Hay |first2=Denys |last3=Scott |first3=John Dick |title=Design and Development of Weapons: Studies in Government and Industrial Organisation |date=1964 |publisher=H.M. Stationery Office |isbn=978-0-11-630089-8 |page=531 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=6rEMAQAAIAAJ |language=en}}</ref>  Helliwells also had government contracts to refurbish and overhaul Boston aircraft as well as Supermarine's [[Spitfire]] and [[Supermarine Seafire|Seafire]] and North American Aviation's [[North American T-6 Texan|Harvard]] in British service.<ref name=smith/><ref>{{cite book |last1=Smith |first1=David John |title=Action Stations: Military airfields of Wales and the North-West |date=1990 |publisher=Stephens |isbn=9781852603755 |page=230 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=o-xmAAAAMAAJ}}</ref>

During this period Eric Sanders, of Dudley-based windscreen company Pearce & Sanders, became managing director and later owner of the company.  He oversaw its transition from domestic supplier to aerospace sub-contractor and its expansion to five factories at Dudley, Walsall and Kings Norton in the West Midlands and in South Wales, employing 5,000 people.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Price |first1=Barrie |title=The Rise of Jaguar |date=2004 |publisher=David and Charles |isbn=978-1-84584-585-8 |page=1929 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=UdMjEQAAQBAJ |language=en}}</ref><ref name=sanders/>  

=== Post-war diversification ===
Shortly after the war Helliwells purchased [[Swallow Sidecar Company|Swallow Coachbuilding]] from [[William Lyons]]' [[Jaguar Cars]] and moved manufacture of Swallow Sidecars to Walsall.<ref name=cooper/><ref>{{cite book |last1=Beaulieu |first1=Edward John Barrington Douglas-Scott-Montagu Baron Montagu of |title=Jaguar |date=1967 |publisher=A. S. Barnes |isbn=978-0-498-06698-6 |page=55 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=Xx5YAAAAMAAJ |language=en}}</ref>  From 1946 they produced the [[Swallow Gadabout]] motor scooter to try to take advantage of an emerging market for cheap scooters.<ref name=science/>  The scooter was designed by Helliwells' chief designer, Frank Rainbow, and was based on the folding [[Welbike]] used by British airborne forces during the war. It had a 125cc 2-stroke [[Villiers Engineering]] engine.  The Gadabout was marketed as the "British Two-wheeler for Mr & Mrs Everyman" and saw service with Staffordshire County Police. A Mark II Gadabout was released in 1949, which remained in production until September 1951, by which time around 2,000 had been manufactured.<ref name=science/><ref name=cooper/> A follow-up model, named the Joyrider was designed but never made.<ref name=science>{{cite web |title=Gadabout Motor Scooter |url=https://collection.sciencemuseumgroup.org.uk/objects/co24487/gadabout-motor-scooter |website=Science Museum Group Collection |access-date=10 October 2024 |language=en}}</ref>  

In 1947 Helliwells announced they were going to manufacture the [[Globe GC-1 Swift]] light aircraft, under licence as the Helliwell Globe but this did not materialise.<ref name=smith>{{cite book |last1=Smith |first1=Ron |title=British Built Aircraft: Central & Eastern England |date=2004 |publisher=Tempus |isbn=978-0-7524-3162-8 |page=204 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=0fy1AAAAIAAJ |language=en |access-date=2024-11-07 |archive-date=2014-06-29 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140629092714/http://books.google.com/books?id=0fY1AAAAIAAJ |url-status=live }}</ref>  During the late 1940s the chairman of [[Standard-Triumph]] [[John Black (businessman)|John Black]] asked Helliwells to build three prototypes of his company's [[Triumph TR-X]] motor car.<ref name=robson>{{cite book |last1=Robson |first2=Richard |first1=Graham|last2=Langworth |title=Triumph Cars - The Complete Story: New Third Edition |date=2018 |publisher=David and Charles |isbn=978-1-78711-689-4 |page=378 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=KdQjEQAAQBAJ |language=ar}}</ref>  Black considered he owed Helliwells a favour for assistance the company had provided to his firm during the war and provided the work as a means of paying them back.<ref name=standard>{{cite book |last1=Robson |first1=Graham |title=The Book of the Standard Motor Company |date=2011 |publisher=David and Charles |isbn=978-1-78711-866-9 |pages=403–404 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=ddMjEQAAQBAJ |language=en}}</ref> Production was slow as Helliwells were not used to motor cars and the prototypes were not completed ahead of the 1949 motor shows they were meant to debut at.<ref name=robson/> The models first appeared at the Paris motor show in 1950 but, despite favourable reviews, did not progress into production and was cancelled in 1951.<ref name=robson/><ref name=standard/>  Two of the three prototypes survive.<ref name=standard/>

Helliwells was sold by Sanders to [[TI Group|Tube Investments Group]] in 1950 and continued as a subsidiary of that firm.<ref name=cooper/><ref name=sanders>{{cite news |title=Obituary Mr Eric Sanders |work=Birmingham Daily Post |date=31 December 1964|page=5}}</ref>  From April 1951 Helliwells had a contract to maintain, overhaul and modify the fleet of the [[Civil Aviation Authority (United Kingdom)|Civil Aviation Flying Unit]] which included [[de Havilland Tiger Moth]]s, [[de Havilland Canada DHC-1 Chipmunk]]s, [[Auster Aircraft]], [[Airspeed Consul]]s, [[Avro Anson|Avro 19s]] and a [[Miles Gemini]].<ref>{{cite book |last1=Woodley |first1=Charles |title=Stansted Airport Through Time |date=15 November 2011 |publisher=Amberley Publishing Limited |isbn=978-1-4456-1106-8 |page=1940 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=boOoAwAAQBAJ |language=en}}</ref>

[[File:1954 Swallow Doretti 2.0 Front.jpg|thumb|The Swallow Doretti]]
In the early 1950s Helliwells management identified demand for a British-style sports car in the American market and looked to develop a vehicle to meet this.  The resulting [[Swallow Doretti]] was based on a 2-litre, 4-cylinder [[Triumph TR2]] engine.  A tubular chassis was used, making the most of in-house manufacturing capabilities.  A high-quality look was achieved with thick carpets and luxury upholstery. The Doretti debuted at the 1953 [[London Motorfair]] with contemporary reviews remarking that it handled better than the TR2.  Sales were launched at the 1954 [[British International Motor Show|Earls Court Motor Show]] with a list price of £777 (plus £324 purchase tax) and an overdrive option available for an addition £56.  This pricing compared unfavourably with the TR2 which was available from £910.  Helliwell's Walsall plant produced 276 Dorettis in 1954 and 1955.  A mark 2 version, to be known as Sabre, was proposed but not progressed.<ref name=cooper/>

=== Later history ===
The company was renamed to TI Helliwells in 1977, to TI Hollow Extrusions in 1985 and to Hollow Extrusions in 1990.<ref name=companies/>  From 2000 it was named Hay Hall Tyseley, after [[Hay Hall, Birmingham]], which until 1998 was occupied by [[Reynolds Technology|Reynolds Tube]], another subsidiary of TI Group.<ref name=companies>{{cite web |title=HAY HALL TYSELEY LIMITED |url=https://find-and-update.company-information.service.gov.uk/company/00062731 |website=Companies House |access-date=11 October 2024 |language=en}}</ref><ref name=acocks>{{cite web |title=Hay Hall |url=https://aghs.jimdofree.com/hay-hall-intro/ |website=Acocks Green History Society |access-date=11 October 2024 |archive-date=24 May 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240524202001/https://aghs.jimdofree.com/hay-hall-intro/ |url-status=live }}</ref>  Hollow Extrusions had been sold by TI in a [[management buyout]] to the former managing director of Reynolds.<ref>{{cite web |title=Today, tomorrow and the next day; Epilogue |url=https://aghs.jimdofree.com/today-future-and-epilogue/ |website=Acocks Green History Society |access-date=11 October 2024 |archive-date=5 December 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20231205214301/https://aghs.jimdofree.com/today-future-and-epilogue/ |url-status=live }}</ref>  The company was dissolved in 2011.<ref name=acocks/>
